Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 serves as an ideal sequel to an already stellar game by refining the things that matter, dropping the things that don’t, and focusing on vastly expanding the blisteringly fast-paced, brutal action.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 not only refines what made the first game good, it polishes out the rough edges, adds more enemies, improves boss fights, brings stronger, grander, more interactive level design, and overall, more 40K. Whether you were a fan of the first Boltgun or diving in now, you're in for a treat.

If you want something you can jump into for a quick gameplay session and have an incredible time blasting through colorful stages and fiendish foes, look no further. Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 delivers fast-paced, exhilarating action that’ll get your heart pumping and your feet stomping. This game gives you that satisfying hit of nostalgia, but with a modern twist that feels charming and unique. With slick gunplay, a brilliant soundtrack, and dozens of tight levels, this is one you won't want to miss.

Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 is bigger and more ambitious than the 2023 original, with a new character, more enemies, weapons and places to go in the non-linear campaign. It remains a highly effective homage to classic boomer shooters and Warhammer 40,000. However, while the battles are bigger and more chaotic, there aren’t many changes of pace and the relentless action becomes a bit repetitive if played too long. Still, it’s hard not to recommend Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 for fans of retro shooters or Games Workshop’s beloved franchise.

Boltgun 2 is a confident, fast-as-hell, modern boomer shooter. With plenty of different ways to purge, fans of the genre will love to embark on a purge fest as either killing machine Malum Caedo or newcomer Nyra Veyrath, Sister of Battle, who is more of a space ninja. The game’s level design and pixelated vistas are particularly impressive. Without overstaying its welcome, Boltgun 2 is a gory, pixel-styled burst of adrenaline, cut into fun, bite-sized missions.

A nurgling genocide of a sequel that directly addresses almost everything that held the first game back, while still finding time to squeeze in a generous dollop of additional creativity. The best ‘90s FPS you never played.
Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 is a solid sequel to a flawed original. It fixes my main issue, with smartly designed levels that help you feel like a proper badass.

Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 firmly establishes itself in the old-school essence of the boomer shooter genre. By introducing a branching campaign structure, heightened verticality in level design, and two playable protagonists with distinct combat styles, the sequel evolves its visceral gameplay, even as it stumbles by setting aside the narrative weight and cinematics of the original title.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 refines what made the first game fun by adding a greater variety of enemies and weapons, and a second, very fun playable character. If you're in the mood for an old-school-style, ultra-violent FPS (and don't mind dealing with dumb enemy AI), Boltgun 2 is for you.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 carries the torch of the original, amplifying its exhilarating gameplay with a compelling new character, detailed enemy and world designs, and level branches that offer a surprising touch of complexity in their objectives. Technical hiccups can lead to moments of frustration that may stunt progress or the flow of action in a few ways. However, the snappy pacing helps keep things moving and context-specific character barks inject personality to round out the gore-geous mess you make in battle. Whether you're a Warhammer die-hard, a classic shooter fan, or simply boomer shooter curious, Boltgun 2 is a genuine blast and well worth your time.

Neon Abyss 2 is a solid addition to today's indie roguelike scene. It manages to stand out thanks to its fun and frantic combat, exploration that encourages experimenting with different builds using randomly discovered items, and challenging enemy design. While its overall structure doesn't feel particularly innovative and its guidance can sometimes be unclear, it's still an experience well worth checking out.
A cracking rogue-like shooter that builds on the solid foundation of the previous game, Neon Abyss 2 offers countless hours of frantic fun.

For better or for worse, Neon Abyss 2 feels very much like more Neon Abyss. But some meaningful changes in progression and permanent upgrades, along with a whole new way to play, make this zany roguelike just as gloriously addictive as the first game ever was.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time with Neon Abyss 2. It’s fun, easy to pick up and play, has a ton of progression systems to keep you hooked, and customization to make runs as easy or hard as you want. I would’ve loved more opportunities to create proper builds rather than having mostly incremental upgrades each run, which could have added an extra layer of complexity that the best-in-class games have.

Neon Abyss 2 is a beautiful sequel, with bolder visuals, flashier weapons and more game-breaking strategies. Unfortunately, the difficulty drops fast once you find the right item combination. The flashy gameplay is fun, but finding a game-breaking strategy happens a bit too quickly. The light show it creates is a joy to behold, yet I couldn’t shake the feeling that I, not the bosses, was the overpowered god of this neon world. A future patch could balance the item drops nicely. Neon Abyss 2 is a great continuation of the franchise that would benefit greatly from some balancing updates. For now, I’ll just go ahead and kill… kill… kill… as I mow through waves of enemies in the variety of game modes on offer. And maybe shoot some hoops with friends in between.

Valor Mortis is the kind of ambitious swing that soulslike fans have dreamed of for years. Witnessing the horrors of war through William’s eyes is one of the best stories brought to the genre in recent memory, and its dark setting of an alternate 19th century Europe carries as much weight as the narrative itself.

The perfect soulslike doesn't exist. There's no such thing, and after so many years of playing them, I'm absolutely sure of it. All of them are bound by shared metroidvania design philosophies and incapacitating issues, and no matter how hard they try, they can never truly surmount them. But Valor Mortis certainly comes dangerously close to doing so, and with gameplay so fluid and a world so fascinating, it's basically as good as they come.

Valor Mortis rarely wastes a beat, producing a surprisingly powerful tale of barbarity that portrays the brutality of war not just through its vicious combat, but through the memory of those who never stood a chance of survival.

Although there is some room for improvement when it comes to refining a few of the technical aspects of the game, Valor Mortis is still a thoroughly engaging experience that left me more than satisfied with my time going through its story and learning about its world. I’m absolutely ecstatic to see what else One More Level has in store for Valor Mortis, and I will definitely be one of the first in line to return for its promised story expansion and New Game+ mode.
Valor Mortis stands out in a saturated genre thanks to its fun combat, excellent level design, and gorgeous visuals.

Valor Mortis is a solid title that kept me hooked for a 20-hour playthrough, delivering a rollercoaster of emotions along the way. To me, that is exactly why Soulslikes have become so popular. The "all-or-nothing" gameplay, high-octane and spectacular combat, and an intriguing setting make this game a standout in the genre, offering a fresh take on a formula that had long since stagnated.

Rather than merely borrowing ideas—from Dark Souls and Dishonored to Sunset Overdrive and even Frogger—One More Level blends them with their own strengths and an original setting to create something truly unique.

Valor Mortis delivers a tense and satisfying first-person soulslike experience, combining strategic combat, rewarding exploration, and a distinctive Napoleonic horror setting. Despite a few technical issues and uneven boss encounters, its strong atmosphere and cohesive mechanics make it a memorable adventure.
Featuring buttery smooth play, fans of first-person melee filled with impactful and meaty combat shouldn't hesitate to check out Valor Mortis.

Forever Ago delivers a deeply moving narrative about aging, grief, and human connection, anchored by soulful voice performances and thoughtful presentation. Its pacing is deliberate, but as one of the most empathetic games of the year, it’s worth hitting the road for this scenic indie title.

Forever Ago is one of those games that left me feeling like I experienced something far greater than its short runtime suggests. Third Shift's debut title tells this genuinely heartfelt story about love, grief, and learning to move forward without leaving the past behind. The occasional technical hiccup is unfortunate, but it never overshadows what the game does so beautifully. Forever Ago is an intimate and moving narrative experience that handles complex themes like aging and loss with rare delicacy. Although its measured pace requires some patience, Third Shift’s title possesses all the warmth needed to win over anyone looking for a profound and reflective story.
Forever Ago is a beautiful tale of loss, grief and growth, and Arthur's roadtrip reminds us all that you just can't plan life.
Forever Ago takes you on an emotional journey to relive the life of a seemingly grumpy old man. It's impressive story-telling that will keep you immersed right through to the end.

Forever Ago is a celebration of life, a beautifully written road-trip on tragedy, love and healing. Despite its technical issues and lack of player agency, it's an example of how walking simulators create unique experiences.

Forever Ago is a quiet, somber yet hopeful exploration of grief, anchored by two wonderful performances in particular, that is unfortunately lacking from a gameplay perspective, but ultimately marks a solid debut for developer Third Shift.

Third Shift’s debut title, Forever Ago, is a remarkable achievement that takes a rare and courageous path in modern development by casting players as an elderly protagonist on a poignant journey through grief, redemption, and meaning, and against all odds, succeeds in crafting an experience that is as deeply reflective as it is charming and peaceful.

Exploration is also its most divisive element: finding your way without waypoints can be genuinely rewarding, but the minimal map and deliberately vague directions can sometimes turn discovery into frustration.

RetroSpace puts humanity’s survival in the hands of a janitor, giving its System Shock-style adventure a blue-collar twist. If you can stomach Retro Space’s cloying satire, and its stifling beholdenment to classic immersive sims, you’ll find a game with sprawling, multilayered systems which smash together in amusing and novel ways.

Amid so many quick cash-ins that prey on nostalgia, this is a remaster done right. Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is a fantastic modernisation that completely overhauls the visuals of the original game while adding smart new features and quality of life improvements, making it just as fun and enthralling as it was a quarter of a century ago.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings a PS2 legend to modern hardware with a complete technical overhaul, rock-solid frame rates, and its iconic cheesy voice acting left completely intact. While old-school map pacing and brutal archers show the game's age, optional modern dodge controls and deep co-op gameplay make it an absolute blast for nostalgia seekers.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is old yet new—a trip down memory lane that’s pure nostalgia from the moment the game starts. It’s a title that never tries to be anything other than what it is, staying true to the essence that made the musou genre popular worldwide.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is a faithful revival that preserves the slower, weightier combat, campy English voice acting, repeated campaigns, and split-screen chaos that defined the original. Its Unreal Engine 5 makeover and modest gameplay additions improve the experience without sanding away its old-school identity, though dated AI, repetition, and occasional technical issues may make it a tougher sell for newer Musou fans.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is the first remaster of the Dynasty Warriors series from Koei Tecmo and Omega Force, and hopefully not the last. While musou games aren’t a groundbreaking genre in 2026, it’s fun to just hack and slash at cannon fodder as you try your best to complete the objective (usually to win). Though, it’s disappointing to see not many updates regarding accessibility features. Regardless, while the formula isn’t new, it’s great for those nostalgic fans and newcomers to the series.

Huge, often empty battlefields are still a chore to traverse, and mowing down hundreds of foes with the same three combos over and over again can be a big ask here in 2026. Still, with so many character stories, unlocks, and game modes to chew on, Remastered earns an easy recommendation if you're a Dynasty Warriors diehard — and I certainly wouldn't be against Koei Tecmo reviving the likes of Dynasty Warriors 4 and 5 in this style.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings the 25 year old classic hack-and-slash title back to life. Fresh lighting and overhauled visuals sparkle, while modern combat elements elevate the slicing and dicing nicely. While there's plenty to cut your teeth on here, the old frustrations with stun-locking enemies, less interesting mission designs and getting crossbow mobbed irk sooner than they should. At least the dialogue is absolutely hilarious and the series' charm remains fully intact.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered achieves its goal of breathing new life into a classic Dynasty Warriors experience, but with no changes to the gameplay, it soon begins to feel too basic and repetitive.

This remaster successfully modernizes a genre-defining classic with impressive visual updates, yet it remains anchored to twenty-five-year-old design limitations. While the simple, repetitive combat provides nostalgic satisfaction for veteran players, the experience inevitably pales in depth and mechanical complexity compared to more modern, refined entries in the series.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings back a true classic in a shiny Unreal Engine 5 coat, delivering an entertaining action game packed with content and a successful visual overhaul. However, it is very much a case of quantity over quality, as the repetitive levels, nonsensical story and lack of depth become increasingly hard to ignore, especially if you don't have nostalgia on your side. As a remaster of a 2001 classic it certainly succeeds, but don't expect any kind of revolution.

Truckful offers a relaxing yet occasionally tense driving experience, combining package deliveries with a mysterious story, side missions, and collectibles. Its engaging narrative and puzzle-based gameplay make exploring enjoyable, although judging the depth of the environment can sometimes be difficult. Despite some grindy Scrap collecting, Truckful delivers a unique and compact adventure.

Truckful is a strange delivery game that shines in its genre mix, blending horror with cozy exploration. However, it also has plenty of speed bumps in its controls and exploration, creating a frustrating driving experience that could use more quality-of-life improvements. Still, once you get past those roadblocks, the game becomes surprisingly heartfelt, with a compelling story and a charming cast of NPCs who stick with you as you unravel the town's mysteries. It’s a bumpy ride, but if you’re willing to stick with it, Truckful is worth taking for a spin.

Truckful‘s flow might be interrupted by frequent loading screens, but it is otherwise a pretty fun, relaxing physics-puzzle about driving through a beautiful countryside delivering packages. That is, until sudden, unexpected but much-appreciated horror elements show up, giving the game a unique and threatening element not present in similar titles.

Truckful has a surprisingly deep, dark story with a lot of enjoyable, entertaining characters. This carried me through the game more than I expected, and I’m glad I got to experience what it had to offer. The physics are hit or miss depending on your driving, but the core mechanics and handling are fun. The game excels in story, world-building, mystery, and, more often than not, the main gameplay loop.

In the long run—much like any video game that simulates a job—Truckful turns into a routine: you end up doing the same things and, for the most part, driving the same roads. You move from one character to another, sometimes just to update them on the situation before speeding off to the next conversation. Car chases become few and far between—save for the showdown with the two ghosts—and the entire cargo-hauling mechanic tends to become monotonous. Ultimately, Truckful is a hard game to pin down: it aims to be "cozy" but fails, as the driving mechanics and camera angles will only frustrate you. It tries to be a thriller, yet that element becomes increasingly muted. It sets out to be a job-simulation game but embraces only the worst possible aspect of the job: the routine. The same faces, the same roads, the same packages—over and over again. At a certain point, you’ll even grow tired of the trees, the tree-lined roads, and the little birds.

An unexpected gem in almost every way. I don't think many were crying out for a Hellraiser game, but everyone will be demanding a sequel to Revival, as Saber's horror show delivers a compelling, rich journey through pain and pleasure.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival is a fantastic game that’ll satisfy both franchise and horror survival fans. Depending on whether or not you can stomach it, of course. It really doesn’t hold back, as it shouldn’t. Between the intense cinematics and the gut-wrenching narrative, this game pulls on every string. The Cenobites of Clive Barker’s world are known for two things: pain and pleasure. And this game showcases it all. There were many times when, while adventuring through the cultists’ underground lair, the world at large, or through the sex club, I had to scrape my jaw off the floor. It is a spectacle, and if you can handle a metric ton of body horror, this game should be on your radar.

Hellraiser: Revival is a faithful adaptation of the universe created by Clive Barker, combining an oppressive atmosphere, grotesque visuals, and genuinely tense moments with a structure heavily inspired by games of the genre, most notably Resident Evil 4 Remake. Although the puzzles are simple and the difficulty decreases considerably as the player masters its mechanics and abilities, the campaign manages to hold its own thanks to the excellent setting, intense chases, and creative use of the Lament Configuration. It's not revolutionary, but it's an interesting and authentic survival horror game for fans of the genre and, especially, of Hellraiser.

Those unfamiliar with Barker’s work who are looking for a strong title in this genre will find one that offers plenty of variety and a striking visual identity. It may not reinvent the wheel, but it knows how to combine its gameplay elements in a highly effective and engaging way.
Hellraiser: Revival is at its best when its horror gamification takes a back seat, providing a world that is equal parts depraved and disturbing, scary and thrilling.
Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival is not for those with weak stomachs. It's also got a lot of painful imagery. If you can power through that, there's a solid survival horror experience underneath.

I am pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed Hellraiser: Revival. Its respect for its source material is apparent throughout, with the Labyrinth, the Cenobites, and the Genesis Configuration being standout pieces of the puzzle. The rest of the game isn't reinventing the wheel for first-person horror, but the "don't fix what isn't broken" approach works just fine here. The squeamish need not apply, as there are moments made to make your skin crawl, but even the most horror-averse people can have a great time in this Labyrinth. Saber Interactive has such sights to show you, and thankfully, there's more pleasure than pain.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival delivers an excellent adaptation by expanding the franchise's mythology and book lore, bringing back the classic voice of Pinhead alongside a bold Unreal Engine 5 art direction. Although it stumbles confusedly between deliberate survival horror and action FPS, the title establishes itself as a worthy adaptation of the series' cultural impact.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival succeeds above all where it matters most: atmosphere, visual identity, and fidelity to the franchise’s aesthetic. The Genesis Configuration adds personality to a fairly traditional survival horror framework, though issues with balancing, AI, and protagonist writing hold back its potential. A successful adaptation, even if not without its rough edges.

It has some issues than can annoy, such as difficulty spikes and a couple of troublesome forced stealth sections, but these don't stop Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival from being a thrilling rollercoaster of a survival horror experience. Sexy, gory and grotesque are perhaps the best words to sum it up.

over the hill is a game that makes you fall in love with it. It challenges you without passing judgment. It gives you freedom while still guiding you through the desire to upgrade your car, and it rewards you whenever you discover something interesting on the map. Above all, Over the Hill is a game brimming with a love for the automotive world—a passion infused into every single polygon.

Over the Hill builds on Art of Rally’s tactile driving and distils the appeal of Saber Interactive’s complex off-roading sims into something much more approachable. The cute animal photography is the cherry on top.

over the hill is a peaceful sandbox game that gives you the freedom to do whatever you want to do. You can play with friends, roam the sandbox together while checking off objectives, or just enjoy your time in the cozy world. Playing alone can make the world feel a bit empty; it still has some kinks to work out, but there’s a very good time to be had just driving around and listening to the radio while you watch the sunset from a peak you just climbed.

The game's performance has been good; while it ran smoothly almost the entire time during our tests on a high-end rig, we do not expect it to perform as well on low-end PCs, given its significant RAM usage.

A few quality-of-life issues could use some work, but otherwise, over the hill reaffirms Funselektor’s knack for creating unusual and engaging driving experiences. Off-roading through the mountains isn’t for everyone, yet the Canadian studio’s latest manages to be accessible to newcomers, offering co-op sessions that can go on for hours without a hitch. If trekking through picturesque landscapes sounds appealing, over the hill will welcome you with open arms.

Ultimately, Over the Hill is a lovely little adventure that understands the simple joy of heading out into the wilderness and seeing what you stumble across. For me, it’s at its best when you’re tackling its trickier trails with friends, where a seemingly straightforward expedition can quickly descend into a chaotic and often hilarious rescue mission where you’ll be eating popcorn by the bucket-load. Progression could do with a little fine-tuning, and I personally don’t find solo play to have quite have the same appeal as multiplayer, but regardless – there’s a lot to like here. If you like the idea of going it alone, or if you’ve got a few friends willing to pile into their 4x4s and head up the trail with you, Over the Hill is well worth the trip.

over the hill offers a fun, easy-going offroading experience. But while I had a good time tackling the terrain both solo and with friends, there’s not a lot to do besides in the beautiful but barren environments. Future updates and DLC may eventually breathe more life into it, but until then over the hill remains a very casual experience that’ll only keep you occupied for brief stints.

While some players may find plenty of enjoyment in over the hill, its multiplayer adds little to the experience. The game looks peaceful, its simplistic art style is charming and the soundtrack fits the intended atmosphere, but frustrating exploration and underwhelming rewards quickly ruin that sense of tranquillity. Bumper Christmas lights are pretty funny, but not when you’ve tumbled down a hill thirty-seven times just to get them.

Almost the anti-driving game. Over The Hill is slow, laborious, and frequently frustrating. The vast game areas are adequately detailed yet oddly empty-feeling. While the expertly curated trial routes are standouts, you're essentially perpetually playing the worst bits of every open world driving game again and again, with little sense of variety or reward.

It's a game gloriously devoid of feature creep or noise, of time limits or competition: a refreshing, head-clearing space. In its quietly rugged way, it's the perfect cozy game. You watch your valiant little 4x4 crawl and bounce across a luscious wilderness as the sun rises and ambient guitar music wafts through the speakers and feel your heart fill with a kind of entranced patience. There's no rush. You'll get there in the end.

Balancing Lunne’s business, relationships, and magical growth as a Heart Witch was one of the best gaming experiences I’ve had all year. With each passing in-game day, I fell more in love with the world and everyone in it. Now, I only want more players to experience the same joy I’ve had with The Witch’s Bakery, so do not let this one go overlooked.

Ultimately, Thank You, Bus Driver is not a full-fledged game in any traditional sense or price. What it actually is may be more important for them right now; an assertion of the passion and creativity that Double Fine have as a developer, no matter what the budget or timeframe. A few hours of chaotic fun delivered with signature charm; it’s more of an entertaining curio than anything else. Even so, it is small, but worthy addition to the Double Fine catalogue for fans of the studio and hopefully – a good sign of things to come.

Thank You Bus Driver delivers a quirky, charming spin on arcade driving with satisfying bus handling, chaotic passenger management, and an inventive 1950s cartoon aesthetic. Its roguelite progression and shifting rules create some entertaining runs, but limited variety, repetitive objectives, and an irritating soundtrack cause the novelty to wear thin long before the journey is over.

Shockwave Triggers is an old-school shooter that is addictive. I love the cooperative approach, the different enemies, and the basic ideas. Despite the lack of depth, I enjoyed the fast-paced and often eye-watering action.

The hypnotic, amphetamine joys of rampaging through cities as a meatball big enough to satisfy god don't last out the whole game, and what Rolla asked of me to see its final levels was  beyond both my skill and patience. But Rolla still executes its simple concept with brilliantly evil flair. There's no fat on this awful meat sphere.

Hungry Horrors, from developer Clumsy Bear Studio, is a card-based joy to play. It’s engaging, wonderfully circular in its design, and an easy game to revisit regularly. The difficulty might turn some gamers away, but once that hill is climbed, it’s a brilliantly built game that will be tough to put down.

The Early Access version of Hungry Horrors is a pretty great introduction to what can be both a unique and incredibly fun title, one that mixes up its own genre with unique mechanics and shows off some very fun character writing and creature designs. I highly recommend this game, even in Early Access, and can’t wait to see what comes with the full release. [Early Access Review]

Deep Dish Dungeon is a fun, quirky little expedition that offers challenging combat and fun food crafting, set in a retro dark fantasy world. Crafting feels immediate and enjoyable, and though the combat may not work for everyone, but if you grew up playing King's Field, it will feel like stepping into a portal to the past.

Deep Dish Dungeon is a game of its time. It taps into the trend of cooperative survival games, successfully connecting with the genre while offering a nostalgic touch by adopting an aesthetic reminiscent of games from bygone eras.
